title: Beyond the Green Light: Why Screen Reader Users Don't Trust Checkboxes
description: Learn how aria-hidden="true" on a checkbox label breaks real-world screen reader experience — even when automated WCAG checks pass.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why WCAG compliance alone may not ensure usability for assistive technology users
Identify how screen readers announce form controls in practice vs. idealized documentation

contentSections.body:
You're reviewing a PR that adds `aria-hidden="true"` to a checkbox's `<label>`, with a comment claiming it 'fixes double-reading' by screen readers. The automated WCAG scan passes with 0 errors — `aria-hidden` on a non-focusable label sibling doesn't trip an automated focusable-hidden-content check. Instead of taking the scan's word for it, turn on your own screen reader — VoiceOver on Mac (`Cmd+F5`) or NVDA on Windows (free, nvaccess.org) — and tab to this checkbox yourself:

```html
<label for="subscribe" aria-hidden="true">Subscribe to our newsletter</label>
<input type="checkbox" id="subscribe">
```

Here's what you'll actually hear when you land on it: 'Checkbox, not checked.' No label, no context. You have no way to know what you're about to check — and neither would anyone else relying on this control the way you're relying on it right now.

**Try it before you read on.** Mac: press `Cmd+F5` to turn on VoiceOver, `Tab` to the checkbox above, then `Ctrl+Option+Right Arrow` to move through it. Windows: download NVDA free at nvaccess.org, launch it, then `Tab` through the same way. Listen for exactly what gets announced when you land on the checkbox — that's your evidence for the question below, not a guess.

You just heard it yourself: automated tools often miss how assistive technologies *actually behave*.

- `aria-hidden="true"` on a `<label>` hides the label entirely from screen readers, but not from sighted users — creating an inconsistent experience.
- Screen readers announce form controls based on DOM order and semantics: labels must be programmatically associated (via `<label for>`, `aria-labelledby`, or wrapping) to be announced *before* the control's state.

The flaw here isn't a missing `alt` text or an empty link — it's breaking core programmatic association. WCAG 2.1 SC 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) can technically pass if an accessible name exists *somewhere* in the DOM, but what you just experienced shows that *how* and *when* the name is announced is what determines whether a user can actually act on it.

contentSections.code:
<label for="subscribe" aria-hidden="true">Subscribe to our newsletter</label>
<input type="checkbox" id="subscribe">
contentSections.question: Based on what you just heard testing this yourself, what's the accessibility flaw in this snippet?

options.label: The input needs an explicit role attribute
aria-hidden on the label hides it from assistive tech
aria-checked must be set explicitly
Keyboard users need an accesskey defined

feedback.aria-hidden-label:
Correct. The `<label>` element is present and correctly associated via `for`/`id`, but `aria-hidden="true"` on it makes that label invisible to screen readers. The input still receives focus and announces 'not checked' — but without the label, the user can't tell what they're checking.

In practice: VoiceOver says *'Subscribe to our newsletter, checkbox, not checked'* only when the label is both programmatically associated **and** visible to assistive tech. Hiding the label defeats the association entirely.
feedback.no-role:
Incorrect. The browser automatically assigns `role="checkbox"` for `<input type="checkbox">` — no need to declare it explicitly.

Even if this were a custom `<div role="checkbox">` widget, the real problem here is the hidden label, not a missing role.
feedback.no-aria-checked:
Incorrect. Native checkboxes auto-manage their checked state; developers shouldn't override it with `aria-checked` unless emulating a checkbox in a fully custom widget (where ARIA state management is genuinely needed).

The actual issue is label visibility to assistive tech, not checked-state reporting.
feedback.no-accesskey: Incorrect. `accesskey` is optional and rarely used in modern accessible design. This snippet fails before a keyboard-only nuance like `accesskey` would even matter — a blind user can't determine what the control does at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This snippet passes an automated scan because `aria-hidden` on a non-focusable label doesn't trip a focusable-hidden-content rule — the failure only surfaces when you actually listen to what gets announced, which is exactly what you just did. The label and input remain structurally associated in the DOM, but that association is worthless once the label itself is removed from the accessibility tree.

contentSections.scenario:
You heard the broken checkbox announce itself with no name at all. The useful next question is which patterns *do* give a control a name a screen reader will read.

Each option below is one checkbox, written a different way. Judge each one on its own.
contentSections.question: Select every checkbox that announces a name when you tab to it.

items.label: A <label for> matching the input id
A <label> wrapping the input, text inside
aria-label on the input
aria-labelledby pointing at a visible span
A <label for> that also has aria-hidden="true"
Text next to the input, with no for and no id

explanation.for-id: Announces a name. `<label for="x">` matched to `<input id="x">` is the association the browser exposes to assistive tech — the version the lesson's broken snippet had, before `aria-hidden` took it away.
explanation.wrapping: Announces a name. Wrapping the input in the `<label>` associates them without needing `for`/`id` at all, so there is no id to typo. It is the pattern that survives the most refactors.
explanation.aria-label: Announces a name. `aria-label` sets the accessible name directly on the input. The cost: there is no visible text tied to it, so a sighted user and a screen reader user are working from two separate strings that can drift apart.
explanation.labelledby: Announces a name. `aria-labelledby` points at the id of an element whose text becomes the name, which is how you reuse text that is already on screen.
explanation.hidden-label: Announces no name. `aria-hidden="true"` removes the label from the accessibility tree, so the association points at something the screen reader can no longer see. This is the exact snippet from the top of this lesson.
explanation.adjacent-text: Announces no name. Sitting next to the input is a visual relationship, not a programmatic one. Sighted users read it as a label; the accessibility tree has no link between the two.

contentSections.synthesis: Four working patterns, two failures — and the two failures look completely fine on screen. That is the shape of this whole category of bug: the name is present in the page and absent from the accessibility tree, and the only way to tell the two apart is to listen.

contentSections.scenario:
A checkbox on a signup form. The visible text reads one thing; the `aria-label` reads another.

```html
<label for="marketing">Email me about new features</label>
<input type="checkbox" id="marketing" aria-label="Marketing opt-in">
```

The control has an accessible name, so it announces something. A voice-input user looking at this page says "click Email me about new features." Nothing happens.
contentSections.question: Is this checkbox compliant?

options.label: Compliant — it has an accessible name
Not compliant — the spoken name drops the visible text
Compliant if the label is also aria-hidden

feedback.label-in-name: Correct. `aria-label` overrides the `<label>` element in the name computation, so the accessible name becomes "Marketing opt-in" and the visible words "Email me about new features" are nowhere in it. Speech-recognition software matches on what the user can read. When the two strings do not overlap, the command has nothing to match, and the user is told the control does not exist.
feedback.compliant: Having a name is not the same as having the right name. The name here is "Marketing opt-in" — a string that appears nowhere on screen. Anyone driving the page by voice reads the visible text aloud and gets no response, which reads to them as a broken page rather than a naming mismatch.
feedback.needs-hidden: Hiding the label would make it worse, not better: the visible text would still be on screen for sighted and voice users, and the mismatch would still be there. It would also strip the one piece of text that describes the control from the accessibility tree.

contentSections.concept:
WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A): where a control has visible label text, its accessible name must contain that text. The order of precedence for the name is `aria-labelledby`, then `aria-label`, then the associated `<label>` — so an `aria-label` added "to be helpful" silently replaces the words on screen rather than adding to them.

The people this hits hardest are not screen reader users. They are voice-input users, and users of speech-to-text on days when typing costs too much. They can see the label perfectly. They say it out loud. The page ignores them.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a checkbox that holds up when someone tabs to it with a screen reader running. Three decisions, one at a time.

fields.prompt: Where does the accessible name come from?

options.label: A <label for> matching the input id
options.value: label[for] matched to the input id

options.label: The text sitting next to the input
options.value: the text next to the input

options.label: The placeholder attribute

fields.correctValue: label[for] matched to the input id

feedback.label[for] matched to the input id: Right — an association the browser exposes to assistive tech, and the same words the sighted user reads. Wrapping the input in the `<label>` works equally well and removes the chance of an id typo.
feedback.the text next to the input: Proximity is a visual convention. Nothing in the markup connects the two, so the control announces its role and state with no name — which is what the broken snippet at the top of this lesson sounded like.
feedback.the placeholder attribute: `<input type="checkbox">` has no placeholder to begin with — the attribute is ignored outright. Even on a text input, a placeholder disappears the moment the user types, which is a poor thing to hang a name on.

fields.prompt: What reports whether the box is checked?

options.label: The native input, maintained by the browser
options.value: the native input, maintained by the browser

options.label: An aria-checked attribute set by JS
options.value: an aria-checked attribute set by JS

options.label: A CSS class the styling reads
options.value: a CSS class the styling reads

fields.correctValue: the native input, maintained by the browser

feedback.the native input, maintained by the brow: Right — a native checkbox keeps its own state and exposes it without any help. Nothing to keep in sync, nothing to forget on a code path you did not think about.
feedback.an aria-checked attribute set by JS: `aria-checked` earns its place in a fully custom widget built from a `<div role="checkbox">`, where nothing else tracks state. On a native input it duplicates what the browser already does, and duplicated state drifts.
feedback.a CSS class the styling reads: A class changes pixels. It does not appear in the accessibility tree, so a screen reader user gets the old state while the screen shows the new one — and nobody testing with their eyes will ever see the gap.

fields.prompt: What counts as proof this works?

options.label: Listening to it with a screen reader
options.value: listening to it with a screen reader

options.label: An automated scan with zero errors
options.value: an automated scan with zero errors

options.label: The label rendering correctly on screen
options.value: the label rendering correctly on screen

fields.correctValue: listening to it with a screen reader

feedback.listening to it with a screen reader: Right — and it takes under a minute per control once the screen reader is already running. You are checking one thing: do the words you hear tell you what you are about to check?
feedback.an automated scan with zero errors: The snippet at the top of this lesson scans clean. `aria-hidden` on a non-focusable label trips no rule, because no rule can tell whether hiding it was deliberate. A green scan narrows what you have to check by hand; it does not replace it.
feedback.the label rendering correctly on screen: This is precisely the check that misses the bug. The label renders perfectly. What broke is invisible on screen and audible in one tab press.

contentSections.synthesis: Native element, native state, verified by ear. The first two decisions are about writing less code, not more — most accessibility failures in form controls come from replacing something the browser already got right. The third is the habit that catches the rest.

contentSections.question: You are auditing one control by hand with a screen reader. Put these steps in the order that actually catches bugs.
steps: Turn the screen reader on (VoiceOver: Cmd+F5, or launch NVDA)
Put the mouse aside — keyboard only from here
Tab until focus lands on the control you are testing
Write down, word for word, what you hear
Compare that against what the screen shows a sighted user
Open the automated scan report last, and see what it missed
contentSections.explanation:
Two orderings matter more than the rest.

The mouse goes away before you start tabbing, not after. Reaching for it once to "get to the right part of the page" skips exactly the stretch of tab order where the bug usually lives.

The scan report comes last. Read it first and you stop testing and start confirming — you go looking for the four things it flagged and hear nothing else. Write down what you heard before you know what a tool expected you to hear, and the gap between the two is the finding.

Writing the announcement down word for word is not bureaucracy. "Checkbox, not checked" and "Subscribe to our newsletter, checkbox, not checked" both round to "it said something" in your memory an hour later. Only one of them is usable.

contentSections.body: WCAG success criteria check for the *technical presence* of an accessible name — you just verified with your own screen reader that users need that name to also be *visible to assistive tech, timely, and unambiguous*, especially on interactive controls like checkboxes. That's the difference between reading a WCAG checklist and doing accessibility QA.

title: Tab Order Is Not Visual Order: A Real-World Keyboard Trap
description: Explore how CSS visual reordering (flexbox, absolute positioning) can silently break keyboard focus order, even when markup uses correct semantic landmarks.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when DOM order conflicts with visual layout and harms keyboard navigation
Differentiate between semantic correctness (e.g. using <nav>) and functional accessibility (a logical focus sequence)

contentSections.body:
Put your mouse aside and tab through this homepage yourself, using only `Tab` (forward) and `Shift+Tab` (back): ```html
…
  • Home
``` CSS visually places `
` above `
` using `flex-direction: column-reverse` on their shared parent — so on screen, the nav bar sits right at the top, exactly where you'd expect it. Start from the top of the page and keep pressing `Tab`, watching where focus actually lands. With your mouse aside, you'll find focus jumps straight into the main article's headings first — no navigation link in sight until much later, if at all. The developer reordered the *pixels*, not the *HTML*, and your keyboard doesn't know or care what the CSS did.

**Try it before you read on.** Mouse away, hands on keyboard only. Starting from the top of a page using this pattern, press `Tab` repeatedly and note exactly where focus goes right after the logo — nav, or straight to the main content? That's your evidence for the question below.

You just felt this yourself: visual layout and focus order are two separate systems, and CSS only controls one of them.

- `flex-direction: row-reverse` or `column-reverse` changes only the *rendered* order — never the tab sequence, which always follows DOM order.
- Absolute positioning used to visually relocate an element (e.g. placing a nav bar visually above main content) has the same problem: focus order is untouched.
- `<nav>`, `<main>`, and other landmarks are genuinely useful for screen reader users — but only for *identifying regions*, not for guaranteeing the order those regions are reached in.

Real assistive-tech behavior: VoiceOver and JAWS announce landmarks as structural regions ('Navigation landmark'), but which one a user reaches *first* when tabbing depends entirely on DOM position — not on how anything looks on screen, as you just confirmed with your own keyboard.

contentSections.scenario:
```html
…
  • Home
``` CSS visually places `
` above `
` using `flex-direction: column-reverse` on their shared parent.
contentSections.question: You just tabbed through this yourself and landed in main before nav. Why does this happen even though nav renders visually first?

options.label: The nav element doesn't have an explicit role attribute
DOM order puts main before nav, so tabbing reaches main first despite visual order
A <ul> isn't allowed inside <nav>
There's no skip-to-main link

feedback.dom-order-mismatch:
Correct. Keyboard and screen reader users encounter content in DOM order — here that means `<main>` before `<nav>`, no matter how CSS visually rearranges them. A user tabbing through the page reaches article headings before ever hitting a navigation link, and may not realize navigation exists at all.

In practice: this is one of the most common real-world accessibility bugs, precisely because it's invisible in a sighted, mouse-driven QA pass — the page *looks* completely correct.
feedback.no-explicit-role: Incorrect. `<nav>` implicitly carries `role="navigation"` — adding it explicitly is harmless but adds nothing. The actual defect is about ordering, not roles.
feedback.invalid-nesting: Incorrect. A `<ul>` inside `<nav>` is exactly the right pattern for grouping navigation links, and satisfies WCAG SC 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships).
feedback.missing-skip-link: Partially relevant but not the core issue. A skip-to-main link helps users bypass repeated navigation on later page visits — it doesn't fix the fact that main content still arrives before navigation in tab order on a first pass.

contentSections.mechanism:
Assistive technology follows the **DOM**, not the visual layout. CSS properties like `flex-direction: column-reverse`, `order`, and `grid-template-areas` change only what is painted on screen — they never reorder the underlying document, so they never reorder focus or the screen reader's reading sequence.

That split is what makes this bug so easy to ship: a sighted, mouse-driven check sees navigation sitting above the article and concludes the page is fine. A keyboard user tabs straight past the article headings before reaching a single navigation link, and a screen reader user hears the page in the same order. Neither of them experiences the layout the designer signed off on.

The fix is to put the elements in the DOM in the order they should be encountered, then use CSS to place them visually — not the other way around. Where the two genuinely must differ, the reading order is the one to preserve.

contentSections.scenario:
A signup form. The CSS reverses the button row, so **Submit renders on the left** and **Clear form** on the right. ```html
Need help?
``` ```css .button-row { display: flex; flex-direction: row-reverse; } ```
contentSections.question: Focus starts at the top of the document, above the form. How many Tab presses before Submit has focus?
contentSections.explanation:
Counting the stops: 1 the "Need help?" link, 2 the name input, 3 the email input, 4 the terms checkbox, 5 **Clear form**, 6 **Submit**.

What is not a stop: `<label>` elements, the `<div class="button-row">`, and the form itself. None of them are focusable, so none of them consume a Tab.

If you counted 5, you counted the page as rendered. `flex-direction: row-reverse` moves Submit to the left of Clear on screen and leaves the tab sequence exactly as the HTML wrote it — Clear first, Submit second. A keyboard user reaches the two buttons in the opposite order from the one they read them in.

This is the everyday version of the failure: not a page that cannot be used, but a page where the destructive-adjacent button arrives before the one the layout presents as primary. The user tabs one stop past where they expected to stop, on a control that clears their work.

contentSections.body:
One more, at whole-page scale. This marketing page has six focusable elements. On screen it renders in the order **header, nav, main** — the navigation sits where anyone would expect it, near the top. ```html Skip to main content
Home
See pricing
Features Docs
``` ```css .page { display: flex; flex-direction: column; } header { order: 1; } nav { order: 2; } main { order: 3; } ``` The `.skip-link` is the usual pattern: hidden off-screen until it takes focus, at which point it becomes visible. Work out where each of the six lands in the tab sequence before you order them below.

contentSections.question: Put the six focusable elements above in the order Tab actually visits them, starting from the top of the document.
steps: Skip to main content link
Home link in the header
See pricing link in main
Start free trial button in main
Features link in the nav
Docs link in the nav
contentSections.explanation:
Tab follows the HTML. The `order` property rearranged three boxes on screen and left the sequence underneath untouched, so `<nav>` renders second and is reached last.

What that costs a keyboard user: they arrive at the page, tab past the header, and land in the body content. Navigation — sitting right there at the top of the screen — is four stops further on, after everything in `<main>`. On a long article, "further on" means dozens of stops. Plenty of people conclude the site has no keyboard-reachable navigation and leave.

The skip link makes it sharper. Its whole job is to let someone bypass the navigation and get to the content. Here the navigation is already after the content, so the link bypasses one header link and nothing else, while the nav it was built to skip stays stranded at the end.

The fix is in the HTML: move `<nav>` above `<main>`, then use `order` to put it wherever the design wants it on screen.

contentSections.scenario: Same page: `<nav>` written after `<main>` in the HTML, rendered above it by CSS. Six proposed changes are on the table in code review.
contentSections.question: Select every change that would actually alter the order focus visits elements.

items.label: Move the <nav> above <main> in the HTML
Add tabindex="1" to each nav link
Set order: -1 on the nav in CSS
Switch the container to flex-direction: row-reverse
Position the nav with position: absolute
Add aria-label="Main navigation" to the nav

explanation.move-dom: Changes it, and it is the fix. Tab order is DOM order, so moving the element is the only change here that addresses the cause. Add `order` afterwards if the design needs the nav somewhere else on screen — now the two agree instead of contradicting each other.
explanation.tabindex-1: Changes it — and creates a worse problem. Any positive `tabindex` is visited before every naturally focusable element on the page, in ascending value order. The nav links would jump ahead of the skip link and the header, and every focusable element added to the page from then on would file in behind them. Positive `tabindex` is the wrong tool even when it appears to work.
explanation.css-order: No effect on focus. `order` is a flexbox painting instruction. It moves the box and leaves the sequence the HTML defined exactly where it was — which is the whole reason this bug exists.
explanation.row-reverse: No effect on focus. Same category as `order`: it reverses what you see, left to right or top to bottom, and the tab sequence keeps following the HTML.
explanation.absolute: No effect on focus. `position: absolute` can move an element to the opposite corner of the viewport without shifting it a single stop in the tab sequence. It is the version of this bug that is hardest to spot in review, because the markup and the screenshot can look unrelated.
explanation.aria-label: No effect on focus. It names the landmark, which genuinely helps a screen reader user who navigates by landmark list. It does nothing for someone moving through the page with Tab, and nothing at all for a sighted keyboard user.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of the six do something, and only one of them is the fix. The pattern worth carrying: no CSS property changes focus order, because focus order is not a visual property. When a reviewer proposes a CSS-only fix for a focus-order bug, that is the tell.

contentSections.scenario:
A password field with a show/hide toggle. The button is absolutely positioned so it sits inside the field's right-hand edge. ```html
``` ```css .field { position: relative; } .field button { position: absolute; right: 8px; top: 50%; } ```
contentSections.question: Does this focus order meet WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order?

options.label: Yes — the toggle comes right after its field
No — absolute positioning breaks focus order
No — the toggle needs a tabindex to be reachable

feedback.meets: Correct. Tab goes to the password field, then to its toggle — which is also the order the two appear in on screen, and the order they make sense in. The absolute positioning moved the button a few pixels inside the field's border and changed nothing about the sequence.
feedback.positioning-breaks: Absolute positioning is not a failure by itself. It fails when it moves an element away from where the HTML puts it in the sequence — a nav painted at the top of the page but written at the bottom. Here the HTML order and the visual order say the same thing, so there is no mismatch to fail on.
feedback.needs-tabindex: `<button>` is focusable with no help. `tabindex="0"` would be redundant, and a positive value would pull it out in front of the rest of the page — the opposite of what this layout needs.

contentSections.concept:
WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A) asks whether the focus sequence preserves meaning and operability. It names no CSS properties, because the property is never the problem.

The question to ask of any layout is narrower than "did we use absolute positioning": **does the order someone tabs through this match the order someone reads it?** When those agree, position, order, and row-reverse are all fine. When they disagree, no CSS change will reconcile them — only editing the HTML will.

Worth naming, since this track is about lived experience rather than rule-matching: a rule that reads as "avoid CSS reordering" produces reviewers who block harmless code and approve the broken kind. The check has to be behavioural, done with a keyboard.

contentSections.body: Semantic markup (using <nav>, <main>) is necessary but not sufficient — keyboard users depend on DOM order for a predictable tab sequence, so always verify focus order by physically tabbing through the page with a keyboard yourself, the way you just did here — not just by checking that landmarks exist.

title: A Modal That Traps Your Mouse but Not Your Keyboard Isn't Accessible
description: A modal dialog can look perfectly functional to a mouse user and still let a keyboard user tab straight out of it into the page behind — a failure invisible unless you actually tab through it yourself.

learningObjectives.text: Test whether a modal dialog correctly traps keyboard focus and restores it on close
Identify the specific keyboard behaviors that distinguish a real focus trap from a visually-modal dialog

contentSections.body:
Open any modal dialog on a site you use often — a cookie consent banner, a signup popup, a confirmation dialog. Before you read further, actually tab through it yourself: click the button that opens it, then press Tab repeatedly, and Shift+Tab, without touching your mouse.

Here's what you're checking for: does focus stay inside the dialog, cycling from the last focusable element back to the first? Or does it eventually escape into the page content sitting behind the dialog — content a sighted mouse user can't see or interact with anyway, because the dialog is visually on top of it, but a keyboard user can now tab into and interact with, invisibly, while the modal still appears open on screen.

**Try it before you read on.** Find a real modal on a site you use. Click to open it, then use only Tab and Shift+Tab. Note exactly what happens when you reach the last focusable element and press Tab again, and what happens when you press Escape.

You just tested this yourself: a modal dialog is only genuinely accessible if it **traps focus** — Tab and Shift+Tab cycle exclusively among the dialog's own focusable elements, never reaching the page behind it, for as long as the dialog is open. This has to be implemented explicitly; it doesn't happen automatically just because a dialog is styled to visually overlay the page. CSS `position: fixed` and a semi-transparent backdrop create a *visual* modal — they do nothing to keyboard tab order, which still follows DOM position exactly as covered in the previous lesson.

Two more behaviors matter beyond the trap itself: focus should land on a sensible element (often the dialog's first focusable control, or the dialog itself) the moment it opens, and pressing Escape should close the dialog *and* return focus to whatever triggered it — not to the top of the page, not left wherever it happened to be. A keyboard user who opened a dialog from a specific button, then closes it, expects to land back at that button, not lose their place entirely.

contentSections.scenario: A modal dialog opens with `position: fixed` and a backdrop overlay. Visually, it fully covers the page behind it. You tab through its three form fields and its Close button — then press Tab one more time.
contentSections.question: What does correctly-implemented focus trapping require happen next, and what would indicate it's broken?

options.label: Focus should wrap back to the dialog's first focusable element; if it instead moves to page content behind the dialog, the trap is broken even though the dialog still looks fully open
Focus should move to the browser's own UI (address bar), since that's outside the page entirely
It doesn't matter where focus goes as long as the dialog still visually covers the page

feedback.wraps-to-first-field: Correct. A real focus trap cycles Tab back to the first focusable element once you pass the last one — the dialog behaves like a closed loop for keyboard purposes. If focus instead lands on an element in the page behind the visually-covering dialog, a keyboard user is now interacting with content they can't see, while the screen still shows the modal as open — exactly the kind of failure that's invisible unless you test with a keyboard yourself.
feedback.escapes-to-browser-chrome: Tab does eventually move focus into browser chrome (the address bar, browser tabs) once it passes the very last focusable element on the whole page — but that's not what a working focus trap should ever let happen. A correctly implemented trap wraps focus back to the dialog's first element long before reaching the end of the document, so the question that actually matters is what happens right after the dialog's last element, inside the page — not whether focus can theoretically reach browser chrome eventually.
feedback.trap-only-relevant-visually: This is exactly the assumption that lets broken focus traps ship — the dialog can look completely fine to anyone testing with a mouse while being fully broken for keyboard-only navigation. Visual appearance and keyboard behavior are two separate things to verify, not one.

contentSections.mechanism: A modal being visually on top of the page (via CSS positioning and a backdrop) has no effect on keyboard tab order, which is governed entirely by JavaScript-managed focus trapping — an explicit implementation choice, not an automatic consequence of visual layering. Testing this requires physically tabbing through the dialog past its last element and confirming focus wraps rather than escapes, the same hands-on verification habit as testing DOM-order tab sequence in the previous lesson.

contentSections.scenario:
A team replaces their hand-rolled modal with the browser's native `` element, on the reasoning that the platform handles focus for them. ```html

Delete this item?

 ``` ```js document.getElementById('confirm').show(); ```
contentSections.question: With the dialog open, where can Tab go?

options.label: Inside the dialog only — <dialog> handles it
Out into the page behind it
Inside, once aria-modal="true" is added

feedback.escapes: Correct. `show()` opens the dialog **non-modally**: the rest of the document stays live and focusable, so Tab walks out of the dialog and into the page behind it — the same failure as the hand-rolled version, reached by a different route. `showModal()` is the method that puts the dialog in the top layer, makes the rest of the document inert, and keeps focus inside.
feedback.stays-inside: `<dialog>` gives you containment only when you open it with `showModal()`. Opened with `show()` — or by putting the `open` attribute in the HTML — it is a visible box with dialog semantics, and Tab leaves it like any other content. One method name is the whole difference.
feedback.needs-aria-modal: `aria-modal="true"` tells a screen reader to keep browse-mode navigation inside the dialog. It has no effect on the Tab key. A dialog with `aria-modal="true"` and nothing containing focus still lets a keyboard user tab straight out.

contentSections.concept:
Modality is two separate mechanisms that get discussed as one thing.

**What a screen reader may reach in browse mode** — controlled by `aria-modal="true"`, or by the inertness `showModal()` applies to the rest of the document.

**Where the Tab key may go** — controlled by containment: the inertness from `showModal()`, the `inert` attribute, or your own JavaScript.

A visual overlay gives you neither. `showModal()` gives you both. `show()` gives you neither, while looking identical on screen to the version that works. Which is why the check is the same one as always: open it, tab past the last control, and watch where focus lands.

contentSections.question: A user activates a "Delete item" button, works through the confirmation dialog, then presses Escape. Put the focus-management steps in the order they have to happen.
steps: Save a reference to the element that opened the dialog
Reveal the dialog
Move focus into the dialog
Contain Tab and Shift+Tab inside the dialog while it is open
Hide the dialog when Escape or Cancel is used
Return focus to the saved element
contentSections.explanation:
Three of these orderings are load-bearing.

**Save the trigger before revealing anything.** Once the dialog opens and focus moves, the element that started this is no longer identifiable from the page state. Capture it at the moment of activation or you have nothing to return to at the last step.

**Reveal before focusing.** A hidden element cannot take focus — `.focus()` on it fails silently, with no error. Get this pair backwards and the dialog opens with focus still parked on the trigger behind it: a screen reader user hears nothing change, and a keyboard user's next Tab continues through the page behind the dialog as though it were not there.

**Hide before restoring focus.** Restore first and the containment from step 4 is still running; it can pull focus straight back in. It also means focus is briefly on something sitting behind a dialog that is still on screen.

Step 6 is the one that gets dropped. Skip it and focus falls back to the document, so the next Tab starts over from the top of the page. Someone who opened this dialog from a button deep in a long list is now at the top of that list, tabbing back down to find their place — and if the answer was "delete," the list they are tabbing through has changed underneath them.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the attributes and behaviours a confirmation dialog needs. Four decisions.

fields.prompt: What identifies this as a dialog to assistive tech?

options.label: role="dialog"
role="alert"
No role — a styled div

feedback.dialog: Right. `role="dialog"` is what tells a screen reader user that a distinct window opened over the page, rather than that some new text appeared. The native `<dialog>` element carries this role already.
feedback.alert: `role="alert"` announces an urgent message as soon as it appears. It does not make a container a dialog, does not imply modality, and on a container full of controls it produces an announcement of the whole thing at once with no structure.
feedback.none: A bare `<div>` is exposed as ordinary grouped content. The dialog appears on screen and nothing signals the change to someone who is not looking at the screen — they tab into a set of controls with no idea a new context opened.

fields.prompt: aria-modal on the dialog container — what value?

options.label: true
false
Omit it — the backdrop covers the page

feedback.true: Right. `aria-modal="true"` marks everything outside the dialog as out of play, so a screen reader keeps browse-mode navigation inside it. Note what it does not do: it has no effect on the Tab key. Containment is a separate job.
feedback.false: `aria-modal="false"` is the default state and states the dialog is not modal. A screen reader user can then arrow out of the dialog and read the page behind it, even with your JavaScript holding the Tab key inside — two navigation modes disagreeing about where the user is.
feedback.omitted: The backdrop is a coloured rectangle. It tells a sighted mouse user the page behind is out of play and communicates nothing to anyone else. Without `aria-modal`, browse-mode reading walks straight out into content the user is being shown as unavailable.

fields.prompt: How does the dialog get its accessible name?

options.label: aria-labelledby, pointing at its heading
The first paragraph of body text
options.value: the first paragraph of body text

options.label: A title attribute on the backdrop
options.value: a title attribute on the backdrop

feedback.aria-labelledby the dialog heading: Right — the `<h2>` is already on screen saying what this dialog is, so pointing at its id reuses it. One string, so the heading and the name cannot drift apart in a later edit.
feedback.the first paragraph of body text: Body text is a description, not a name, and it is usually a sentence or two long. "This action cannot be undone and will remove the item from every list it appears in" is what a user would hear where they expected a title.
feedback.a title attribute on the backdrop: The backdrop is not the dialog, so a name on it names the wrong element. The dialog itself would still be unnamed.

fields.prompt: When the dialog closes, focus goes to...

options.label: The element that opened it
The top of the page
Wherever it happened to be

feedback.the element that opened it: Right. The user gets back the place they were working from, which is the difference between a dialog being an interruption and being a detour that costs them their position on the page.
feedback.the top of the page: This is what happens by default when nothing restores focus, and it is a real cost: someone who opened the dialog from a button forty stops down is now tabbing forty stops back. On a page whose content the dialog changed, they are doing that through a list that no longer matches their memory of it.
feedback.wherever it happened to be: Focus cannot stay where it was — where it was is inside a dialog that no longer exists. When the focused element is removed, focus falls back to the document, which is the top-of-the-page case under a different name.

contentSections.synthesis:
Role, modality, name, and focus restoration — four things a hand-rolled modal has to get right individually, plus the Tab containment from the previous exercise.

The native `<dialog>` element opened with `showModal()` supplies the dialog role, the inertness that both contains Tab and keeps browse-mode inside, and focus restoration on `close()`. You still supply the accessible name, and you still verify the rest yourself — this lesson exists because "the platform handles it" is the assumption that ships broken dialogs.

contentSections.scenario: The dialog is built, it renders correctly, and the automated scan is clean. You have it open in front of you with your hands on the keyboard.
contentSections.question: Select every check that has to be done by hand before you call this dialog accessible.

items.label: Tab from the last control returns to the first
Shift+Tab from the first control returns to the last
Escape closes the dialog
Focus returns to the button that opened it
The backdrop dims the page behind it
Clicking outside the dialog closes it

explanation.tab-wraps: Check it. This is the containment the lesson opened with, and the direction everyone tests. If focus lands on page content instead, the user is now typing into something the screen is covering.
explanation.shift-tab-wraps: Check it — and check it second, because it is the direction that gets forgotten. A trap written only for the forward case lets Shift+Tab from the first control walk backwards into the page. It looks fixed from one direction and is broken from the other.
explanation.escape-closes: Check it. Escape is the keyboard user's way out. Without it, someone whose pointer is unreliable — tremor, one-handed use, a bad pain day — is held in a dialog until they find a Close button that focus may or may not reach.
explanation.focus-returns: Check it. Closing the dialog is only half the interaction; the other half is landing back where you were. Verify it by noting which button you opened it from and looking at where focus sits after it closes.
explanation.backdrop-dims: Not a check — this is the thing that lets the bug through review. A dimmed backdrop tells a sighted mouse user the page behind is out of play and tells a keyboard user nothing at all. Every broken modal in this lesson has a perfectly good backdrop.
explanation.click-outside: Not a check. It is a mouse convenience, and a keyboard-only user has no "outside" to click, so it proves nothing about whether they can get out. Escape is the equivalent that matters, and that one is on the list.

contentSections.synthesis:
Four checks, roughly thirty seconds, no tooling beyond the keyboard already in front of you. None of the four appear in an automated scan report, because each of them is a question about behaviour over time rather than about markup at a moment.

The two that are not checks share a property worth noticing: both are things you verify with a mouse. Anything you can confirm with a mouse is, by definition, not telling you about the experience this lesson is about.

contentSections.body: A modal that looks completely functional to a mouse user can still be broken for keyboard users in a way that's invisible unless you tab through it yourself, past the last element, and check where focus actually goes. That's the specific, concrete check — not "does the dialog look right" but "does Tab wrap inside it, and does Escape return focus to where you started."

title: A Barrier Is Not an Inconvenience: What Actually Goes in the Ticket
description: Two findings can look equally annoying and be completely different severities — the test is whether a task gets blocked, not whether something is mildly irritating, and the language you file it in decides whether it gets fixed.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a genuine access barrier from an inconvenience using a task-completion test rather than a personal-annoyance one
Explain how the medical and social models of disability lead to different defect write-ups for the same underlying bug, and why that difference changes triage priority

contentSections.body:
You're two weeks into scoping the audit for Havenmark, a mid-size Dutch home-and-lifestyle retailer bracing for European Accessibility Act enforcement. Your intake notes have two findings sitting side by side from the same product page:

1. The "−15% today" sale badge renders in white text on a light-pink background — you measured it at 3.2:1 contrast, and you use a screen magnifier on bad days because sustained close focus triggers eye strain; you had to zoom to 300% and squint to read it at all.
2. The product-quantity stepper's font is Havenmark's in-house typeface, which you personally find a little cramped and don't love the look of.

Both are things about the page you noticed and didn't enjoy. Only one belongs in the audit as a defect. If you can't say which, and why, in one sentence, the rest of the audit inherits the fuzziness — every finding after this one gets judged by "does this bother someone" instead of a test that holds up when someone else re-runs it.

**The test that separates the two**: does this prevent an equivalent user from completing the task, or does it make completion cost meaningfully more — more time, more re-reading, more physical effort, more risk of error — than it costs someone without the condition? If yes, it's a barrier. If the friction is minor, evenly distributed across everyone regardless of ability, and doesn't block the task, it's an inconvenience: real, worth a design-polish ticket maybe, but not an accessibility defect.

The sale badge fails WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum, Level AA) outright — 3.2:1 against a 4.5:1 requirement for normal-size text. That's not a style preference; a specific, measurable class of users — anyone with low vision, anyone reading on a washed-out phone screen in daylight, anyone whose eyes fatigue faster than average — cannot reliably read "−15% today" at all. The task (know the discount before you decide to buy) is blocked for them and not for a full-vision user in ideal lighting. That asymmetry is the barrier.

The typeface you find cramped is an aesthetic reaction. It doesn't block reading for a defined class of users more than it blocks it for anyone else — if it's genuinely hard to read at small sizes, that's a different, testable claim (measure x-height, character spacing) and a different finding. "I don't like it" isn't that claim, and writing it up as one teaches whoever reads your reports that accessibility findings are partly a matter of taste — which is exactly the reputation this field is fighting.

**Why the same bug gets written up two different ways.** The medical model of disability treats disability as a property of the person — something located in their body or mind, a deficit to be accommodated as an exception. The social model treats disability as what happens when an environment built for a narrow assumed "typical" user meets a body or mind it wasn't built for — the barrier is in the design, not the person.

This isn't an abstract debate; it changes what you type into the ticket. Take the sale badge again. Write it the medical-model way: *"Blind and low-vision users may struggle to read the discount badge."* That sentence puts the limitation in the user — it reads as a fact about them, and it reads as an edge case, because it names a specific minority of users as the ones affected. Write it the social-model way: *"The discount badge renders at 3.2:1 contrast against a 4.5:1 minimum (WCAG 1.4.3), making it unreadable for any user without full-contrast vision in good lighting — including low-vision users, older users, and anyone viewing the page in bright light or on a dimmed screen."* Same underlying bug. The second version puts the defect in the component, states the population affected in a way that includes situational users a triage meeting will recognize immediately, and gives a fix target (raise the contrast ratio) instead of an accommodation request.

Teams that inherit medical-model tickets tend to route them to a backlog reserved for "accessibility asks" — nice to have, low priority, revisit next quarter. Teams that inherit social-model tickets route them the way they'd route any other broken component, because that's what the ticket says it is.

contentSections.scenario:
Two draft tickets for the same underlying bug at Havenmark — a size-guide link inside the product page that opens as an image-only PDF with no text layer, so it doesn't work with a screen reader's "find in page" or with a magnifier's reflow.

Draft A: "Blind users can't access the size guide, since screen readers can't read image-based PDFs."

Draft B: "Size guide is an image-only PDF with no text layer or alt content — fails WCAG 1.1.1 (Non-text Content). Unusable with a screen reader, unusable with browser zoom/reflow for low-vision users, and won't index for anyone using in-page search. Fix: publish as an accessible HTML table, or a tagged PDF with a real text layer."
contentSections.question: You have limited review time and can only push one of these two into the sprint. Which framing is more likely to actually get the fix scheduled, and why?

options.label: Draft B — it names the failing criterion, the full population affected, and a fix target, so it reads as a broken component
Draft A — naming the specific affected group builds more empathy with the team and gets prioritized faster
Both are equivalent — engineering teams triage by severity, not by how the ticket is worded

feedback.draft-b-scope: Correct. Draft B cites the specific success criterion (so it's not arguable as opinion), names three separate user groups affected by the same root cause (so it doesn't read as an edge case), and states the fix in the same sentence (so triage doesn't stall on "what would we even do about this"). It reads exactly like any other P1 bug report — because that's what it is.
feedback.draft-a-empathy: This is the tempting answer, but it backfires in practice: naming one group in isolation is precisely what makes a ticket read as an accommodation request rather than a defect — reviewers unconsciously ask "how many users does this affect" and a single named group, with no criterion cited, sounds small even when it isn't. Draft A also omits that low-vision and search-dependent users hit the identical bug, which understates the actual scope.
feedback.both-same: Ticket wording measurably changes triage outcomes — this is a well-documented pattern in accessibility program management, not a matter of team culture. A ticket that reads as "a group of users has a problem" and a ticket that reads as "this component is broken" get routed to different queues even inside the same team, because they're answering different questions ("should we help them" vs "is this shipped broken").

contentSections.concept: The medical model locates the problem in the user and produces tickets that read as requests for accommodation. The social model locates the problem in the design and produces tickets that read as defect reports. Both descriptions can be factually accurate about the same bug — the choice of framing is not about honesty, it's about which one gets scheduled. As the auditor, you choose the framing every time you write a finding down, whether you're conscious of it or not.

contentSections.scenario: Four more findings from the same Havenmark audit pass. For each, apply the task-completion test: does it block or meaningfully burden a defined class of users relative to everyone else, or is it minor friction spread evenly?
contentSections.question: Select every finding that is a genuine barrier, not an inconvenience.

items.label: Homepage carousel auto-advances every 4 seconds with no pause control, restarting screen reader announcements before a user with slower reading speed can finish the current slide
Quantity stepper's + button measures 20×20 CSS px against WCAG 2.2's 24×24 px minimum (SC 2.5.8) — testers with hand tremor missed it on 6 of 10 attempts
Havenmark's brand red is a slightly different shade than the one used in last year's campaign photography
Checkout form shows a red asterisk next to invalid fields but no text describing what's wrong, so a screen reader announces nothing about which field failed or why
Page-load spinner animates slightly faster than the design spec called for

Product demo video has burned-in captions in a font some testers describe as slightly too small for comfortable reading, though all wording is legible at 100% zoom for testers without a vision condition

explanation.carousel-autoplay: Barrier. This fails WCAG 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide) — content that auto-updates and lasts longer than 5 seconds must be pausable. Anyone who reads slower than the carousel's pace — including cognitive processing differences, screen magnification, or simply a bad brain-fog day — never finishes a slide before it's replaced. The task (learn what's on offer) is blocked for a defined class of users and isn't for a fast, unaided reader.
explanation.tap-target: Barrier. This is a below-minimum target size (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8, Level AA) with a measured failure rate for tremor users. "Testers missed it 6 of 10 times" is a task-completion failure, not an annoyance — the task (add the item to cart) doesn't complete.
explanation.brand-color: Inconvenience, and arguably not even that — it's a brand-consistency note, not an access issue. No class of user is blocked or burdened relative to any other by a slightly different shade of red.
explanation.form-error: Barrier. This fails WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) and 3.3.1 (Error Identification) — a screen reader user gets no indication a field failed at all, let alone which one or why. A sighted user sees a red asterisk (itself a weak signal, but a signal); a screen reader user gets nothing. The checkout task is blocked for one group and not the other.
explanation.loading-spinner: Inconvenience. A few hundred milliseconds' difference in animation speed against a design spec is a QA note for the design team, not an accessibility finding — it doesn't change who can complete the task.
explanation.video-captions: Borderline, and here it's an inconvenience: the wording states captions are legible at 100% zoom for testers without a vision condition, meaning the task (read the captions) completes for the comparison group too — this is a preference about comfort, not a completion failure. Note the wording carefully: if testers with low vision specifically couldn't read them, or the caption text failed a measured contrast or size threshold, this would flip to a barrier. The test doesn't change; only the evidence does.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of six are barriers, and all three cite a specific success criterion, a specific mechanism of exclusion, and — where available — a measured failure rate. The three that aren't barriers share the opposite shape: no defined population is blocked relative to another, just a general preference or a QA-level polish note. When a finding won't fit that shape, that's the signal to keep testing rather than to write the ticket.

contentSections.body: A barrier blocks a task, or meaningfully raises its cost, for a defined class of users relative to everyone else — measured against a success criterion, not against your own taste. And the same true bug can be written up two ways: as something wrong with a user, or as something wrong with a component. Write it as the second one. That's not spin — it's accuracy about where the defect actually lives, and it's the difference between a finding that gets fixed and one that gets filed away as a favor to a minority of users.

title: The Access Needs a Screen Reader Demo Never Shows You
description: Blindness is the access need every intro deck demonstrates. Motor, cognitive, vestibular, chronic-pain, and situational needs are the ones that actually make up most of an audit — and most of the auditors doing the work.

learningObjectives.text: Identify access needs across sensory, motor, cognitive, vestibular, chronic-pain/fatigue, and situational categories using concrete page elements
Map a specific interface pattern to the WCAG success criteria that govern it for non-visual access needs

contentSections.body:
Today's Havenmark task is the checkout flow, and today is not a good day. Brain fog is heavy — the kind where a five-field form takes real, deliberate effort to hold in your head, and where you have to reread the same line twice before it lands. You open the page and immediately hit two things: a banner reading "Complete your order in 09:58 or your cart will be cleared," counting down live, and an auto-rotating "customers also viewed" carousel with a parallax scroll effect sliding underneath it as you scroll past.

You are not testing this as a hypothetical blind user with a screen reader — the demo every accessibility 101 deck opens with. You are testing it as yourself, on a day your own body has already told you something about, before you've read a single line of WCAG. That's not a compromised test. It's the test this track exists to teach: you are frequently the assistive-technology user, and the barriers that stop you are real audit findings, not personal problems to push through.

**Vision** is the access need every training deck leads with, because it's the easiest to demo — put on a blindfold, turn on a screen reader, done. It's real, and it's a fraction of what an audit has to cover.

**Motor**: tremor, limited fine motor control, one-handed use (temporary or permanent), switch access, voice control. A 20×20px tap target that a mouse user clears without noticing is a real miss rate for someone with tremor — WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 sets a 24×24px minimum for exactly this reason. Voice-control users (Dragon, Voice Control on iOS/macOS) issue commands that match visible text — a button whose accessible name doesn't match its visible label, covered in an earlier lesson, breaks for them specifically, distinct from how it breaks for a screen reader user.

**Cognitive**: memory, executive function, processing speed, reading level. A countdown timer with no way to extend it (failing WCAG SC 2.2.1, Timing Adjustable) doesn't just inconvenience — it actively punishes anyone who needs more time to read, decide, or recheck a form, converting a cognitive difference into a lost cart. WCAG SC 3.1.5 (Reading Level, AAA) exists because dense, jargon-heavy copy is a genuine barrier for cognitive and learning differences, not just a style note.

**Vestibular**: motion sensitivity, where parallax scrolling, auto-playing video backgrounds, and large animated transitions cause real physical symptoms — dizziness, nausea, disorientation — not mere distraction. WCAG SC 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions, AAA) asks that motion triggered by interaction can be disabled; `prefers-reduced-motion` is the practical mechanism a site can honor.

**Chronic pain and fatigue**: unpredictable energy, unpredictable typing speed and accuracy, the real cost of a form that can't be saved partway through, the real cost of a session timeout that doesn't account for someone who has to stop and rest mid-task. This category rarely gets a dedicated WCAG success criterion by name — it shows up as timing (2.2.1), as save state, as error tolerance (3.3.4 Error Prevention). It's frequently invisible in a lived-experience audit precisely because the auditor pushes through it rather than logging it as data.

**Temporary and situational**: a broken wrist in a cast, screen glare on a phone outdoors, holding a baby in one arm, a shared office where audio has to stay off, a train with no signal reloading a half-filled form. These aren't edge cases either — they're the same barriers as permanent motor, vestibular, and low-vision needs, just with a different duration. A one-handed checkout flow serves someone with a permanent condition and someone with a temporary cast identically; the fix doesn't know or care which.

contentSections.scenario: Six findings from today's Havenmark checkout pass, logged as you worked through the flow on a heavy brain-fog day. Match each one to the WCAG success criterion category it actually falls under before you write it up.
contentSections.question: Select every finding that maps to a timing- or motion-related success criterion (2.2.1, 2.2.2, or 2.3.x) rather than a different category.

items.label: "Complete your order in 09:58" countdown with no visible way to extend or disable it
Auto-rotating product carousel with a parallax scroll effect and no pause control
Session silently expires after 10 minutes of inactivity, discarding the entire cart with no warning beforehand
"Apply promo code" button whose accessible name is set to "btn-promo-42" by a build tool, so voice-control users saying "click apply promo code" get no match
Form submission fails silently with red field outlines only — no text listing what needs fixing
Shipping options described only as "Expedited Tier 2 Fulfillment" with no plain-language explanation of what that means or costs

explanation.countdown-no-extend: Applicable. This is a direct SC 2.2.1 (Timing Adjustable) failure — a time limit with no way to turn it off, adjust it, or extend it. It's a timing-category finding, and it's the clearest one in this batch.
explanation.carousel-parallax: Applicable. This spans two categories: SC 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide) because it auto-updates with no pause control, and it's also a vestibular-trigger concern under SC 2.3.3 territory because of the parallax motion. Flag both mechanisms in the same finding rather than picking one.
explanation.session-drop-noexplain: Applicable. A silent, unwarned timeout is squarely SC 2.2.1 — the fix isn't just extending the limit, it's warning the user before it fires and letting them extend it with one action, which the criterion specifically requires.
explanation.field-label-mismatch: Not a timing/motion finding — this is a name-role-value problem (SC 4.1.2 territory, and specifically SC 2.5.3 Label in Name for the voice-control mismatch), the same failure category covered in an earlier lesson. Motor/voice-control access need, wrong SC category for this question.
explanation.no-error-summary: Not a timing/motion finding — this is SC 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 4.1.2 territory: the accessible name and state of the error aren't communicated. Cognitive and screen-reader access need, wrong category here.
explanation.dense-jargon: Not a timing/motion finding — this is SC 3.1.5 (Reading Level) and plain-language territory, a cognitive-access finding about comprehension, not about time or movement.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of six genuinely belong to the timing/motion cluster; the other three are real findings too, just filed under different criteria — label/name issues, error identification, and reading level. An audit report that lumps all six under one vague "accessibility issues" heading loses exactly the information a developer needs to know which fix pattern applies. Naming the right SC category per finding is part of what makes the report actionable rather than just a list of complaints.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's product manager reviews your findings list and pushes back on one: "the 10-minute checkout timer only affects a tiny edge case — most people finish checkout in under two minutes." You have your own testing notes from today: brain fog made a normally 90-second form take you closer to 14 minutes, including two full re-reads of the shipping section because you'd lost your place.
contentSections.question: What's the strongest response to "most people finish in under two minutes, so this is an edge case"?

options.label: The relevant question isn't how many people are affected on average — it's whether the design fails a defined, real, and non-trivial population predictably, which SC 2.2.1 exists specifically to protect regardless of what the average user does
The PM's two-minute average is probably inflated and should be re-measured before the finding is dismissed
Accept it's an edge case but ask for it to be fixed anyway as a goodwill gesture

feedback.reframe-who-not-how-many: Correct. WCAG success criteria aren't written around the median user's experience — they exist because a design that works for the median user can still reliably fail a specific, definable population, and "reliably fail some real group of users" is the bar, not "fail most users." Your own testing data — a 90-second task taking 14 minutes on a real, reproducible cognitive-load day — is exactly the kind of first-person evidence that makes this concrete rather than theoretical. This finding doesn't need a bigger affected-population estimate to be valid; it needs to be understood as measuring against the wrong baseline.
feedback.average-is-wrong: This concedes the PM's frame — that population size is the deciding factor — which is the wrong argument to win. Even if the two-minute average is accurate, that number describes users without the conditions SC 2.2.1 exists to protect. Arguing about the average sidesteps the actual point.
feedback.concede-edge-case: This also concedes the frame, and worse, it downgrades a WCAG Level A failure to a favor. SC 2.2.1 is not optional politeness extended to a minority — it's a baseline conformance requirement, and calling it an edge case in the ticket is exactly the medical-model framing from the previous lesson, applied here to timing instead of contrast.

contentSections.concept: "How many people does this affect" is the wrong question for a conformance finding, and it's a question worth being ready to redirect in the room, not just in the ticket. The right question is whether the design predictably fails a definable population under normal conditions — and your own lived data, logged in the moment rather than reconstructed afterward, is some of the strongest evidence available for answering it.

contentSections.body: Blindness is the easiest access need to demo and the smallest slice of what an audit has to cover. Motor, cognitive, vestibular, chronic-pain/fatigue, and situational needs make up most of the real findings — and most of the auditors who catch them are drawing on their own bodies as the test instrument, on their own bad days, not simulating someone else's. That's not a limitation on the work. It's the source of findings a purely automated or purely able-bodied review would never produce.

title: Why Automated Scanners Catch About a Third of the Barriers That Matter
description: Havenmark's dev team runs axe-core in CI and gets zero errors on a size-picker that's completely unusable by keyboard — understanding exactly why closes the gap between a green scan and a real audit.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the structural reasons automated accessibility scanners can verify some WCAG success criteria but not others
Sequence an audit workflow that uses automated scanning for triage without mistaking it for the audit itself

contentSections.body:
Havenmark's lead developer messages you before your first full audit session: "Heads up — we run axe-core in CI on every PR and we're at zero critical issues sitewide. Not sure how much your audit is going to find." You open the product page and go straight to the size picker: a row of custom `<div>` elements styled to look like buttons, each one a size (XS, S, M, L, XL). You put your mouse aside and press Tab. Focus skips the entire row — none of the divs are reachable by keyboard at all. A user who can't operate a mouse cannot select a size, which means they cannot buy a single item on this site.

The scan Havenmark runs in CI reported zero critical issues on this exact page. It isn't wrong, exactly — it's answering a narrower question than "can everyone complete this task," and the gap between those two questions is the entire reason this job exists as a job, rather than as a script.

**What automated scanners are genuinely good at**: syntactic and structural checks against machine-verifiable rules. Missing `alt` attributes, contrast ratios against solid backgrounds, duplicate `id` values, missing form labels where no label element exists at all, invalid ARIA attribute values, heading levels that skip (`h2` straight to `h4`). These are things a program can check by parsing the DOM and applying a rule — no judgment required, and scanners do this fast, consistently, and at a scale no human review can match. Running one in CI on every PR is a genuinely good practice, and this lesson isn't an argument against doing it. **What they structurally can't verify**, because it requires understanding rather than pattern-matching: - **Whether an accessible name is any good.** `alt="image1.jpg"` and `alt="Woman wearing the navy wool coat, side view"` both pass a scan — both are non-empty `alt` attributes on `` tags, satisfying SC 1.1.1 syntactically. Only one actually describes the image. - **Whether a custom widget is keyboard-operable.** The size-picker `
`s aren't invalid HTML — they're valid, unstyled `
` elements with no interactive semantics, and a scanner has no rule that says "this should have been a button" because plenty of `
`s legitimately aren't interactive. Detecting this requires knowing what the element is supposed to do, which is exactly the judgment a scanner doesn't have. - **Whether focus order or a focus trap actually work.** Both of the earlier lessons in this module — DOM order versus visual order, and modal focus trapping — describe failures that require pressing Tab and watching where focus goes over time. A scan reads a static DOM tree; it doesn't press keys. - **Whether motion, timing, or cognitive load cross a real threshold.** A parallax carousel and a ten-minute countdown timer are both intentional features, built exactly as specified — there's no malformed markup for a scanner to flag. - **Whether the page makes sense read as a whole.** Heading structure can be technically valid and still fail to represent the actual content hierarchy in a way that supports screen-reader navigation by headings. Put a number on it, because "scanners miss some stuff" undersells the gap: testing-tool vendors' own documentation puts automated coverage at roughly 30-40% of WCAG success criteria — call it a third. The other two-thirds require a human operating real assistive technology, which is exactly the audit you're running.

contentSections.scenario:
The Havenmark size-picker: six `
XS
` elements, styled with CSS to look like buttons, with a JavaScript `click` listener attached to each. axe-core reports zero errors on this component.
contentSections.question: Why doesn't the scanner flag this, given that the component is completely unusable by keyboard?

options.label: A <div> with a click handler is syntactically valid HTML — the scanner has no rule for "this element's apparent purpose doesn't match its semantics," because that requires understanding what the component is for, not just parsing what it is
This is a bug in axe-core specifically — a more thorough scanner would catch it
The CSS styling is what's hiding the issue from the scanner

feedback.no-rule-can-know-intent: Correct. There is nothing malformed about a `<div>` with a click handler — millions of legitimate `<div>`s on the web have click handlers for things that don't need keyboard operability (a decorative hover effect, for instance). The scanner would have to know that *this specific* set of divs represents the only way to select a required product option, which is a judgment about purpose and context that no DOM-parsing rule can make. That judgment is exactly what a human tester supplies by trying to complete the task with a keyboard.
feedback.scanner-bug: This isn't a bug to be patched — it's a structural limit of what pattern-matching against markup can determine. Every major automated scanner (axe-core, WAVE, Lighthouse) has this same blind spot for the same reason: none of them can infer intent from valid-but-wrong markup.
feedback.css-styling-hides-it: CSS styling changes what the element looks like, not what the scanner reads. The scanner analyzes the DOM and accessibility tree, which are unaffected by how something is painted on screen — this is the same DOM-versus-render distinction from the tab-order lesson, applied to a different bug.

contentSections.mechanism: Automated scanners work by pattern-matching the DOM against a rule set: does this attribute exist, is this value in a valid range, is this relationship present. Anything that requires knowing what a component is supposed to do — versus what it technically is — sits outside that rule set by construction, not by an oversight anyone could patch. That's the real dividing line between the roughly one-third of issues scanners catch and the two-thirds they don't: syntactic validity versus functional correctness.

contentSections.question: You're scoping the full audit workflow for Havenmark's checkout flow, from a cold start. Put these steps in the order that uses the automated scan for what it's good at, without mistaking it for the audit.
steps: Run the automated scanner across the flow to triage the syntactic, high-volume issues (missing alt text, contrast failures, missing labels) fast
Fix or file the automated findings so they stop consuming attention during manual passes
Tab through the entire flow keyboard-only, noting every point focus is lost, trapped incorrectly, or visually out of sync with DOM order
Run the flow with a screen reader, listening for accessible names, redundant announcements, and unlabeled state changes
Test against your own access needs and any team members' or user panel's differing needs — motor, cognitive, vestibular, chronic-pain/fatigue, situational
Write findings classifying each as a barrier or inconvenience, citing the specific WCAG success criterion, before compiling the report
contentSections.explanation:
The scan goes first because it's fast and cheap, and clearing the high-volume syntactic issues out of the way means the manual passes aren't repeatedly interrupted by things a machine already caught — that's the scan's real value, triage, not verdict.

Keyboard-only comes before screen reader testing because a component that isn't keyboard-operable at all usually can't be meaningfully screen-reader tested either — you can't evaluate what a screen reader announces on focus for an element that never receives focus. Fixing or at least flagging keyboard gaps first makes the screen-reader pass more informative.

Testing against a range of access needs — not just the screen-reader case — comes after the two most "instrumented" passes, because it's where findings the previous two passes structurally can't produce show up: timing, motion, cognitive load, physical effort. This is the step most audits compress or skip when time is short, and it's usually where the highest-value findings live, precisely because it's the step a scan and a rote keyboard/screen-reader checklist both miss.

Writing findings last, with the barrier/inconvenience classification and cited criterion from the earlier lessons in this module, is what turns a session's worth of observations into a report someone can act on instead of a pile of notes.

contentSections.scenario: A batch of findings from the Havenmark audit. For each, decide whether an automated scanner running against this exact page would catch it.
contentSections.question: Select every finding an automated scanner would reliably catch.

items.label: Product thumbnail images have no alt attribute at all
Sale badge text at 3.2:1 contrast against a solid background color
Two elements on the page share id="email"
Product image alt text reads "image_047.jpg"
Modal dialog doesn't trap focus — Tab escapes into the page behind it
CSS visually reorders nav above main, but DOM order puts main first

explanation.missing-alt: Caught. A completely absent alt attribute on an is a direct, syntactic rule violation — exactly the class of check scanners are reliable at.
explanation.low-contrast-solid: Caught. Contrast ratio against a solid, computable background color is arithmetic a scanner can perform directly from rendered CSS values.
explanation.duplicate-ids: Caught. Parsing the DOM for repeated id attribute values is a straightforward structural check.
explanation.useless-alt-text: Missed. The attribute is present and non-empty, which is all a scanner checks — it has no way to evaluate whether the text describes the image, because that requires understanding the image's content and the text's meaning, not just its presence.
explanation.keyboard-trap-missing: Missed. This requires simulating a Tab-key sequence over time and checking where focus lands relative to the dialog's boundary — a scan of the static DOM has no notion of a keypress sequence or of "while this dialog is open."
explanation.reading-order-mismatch: Missed. Both the DOM order and the CSS are individually valid; the failure only exists in the mismatch between what's rendered and what's read, which requires comparing visual layout to DOM position — a comparison outside a rule-based structural scan.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of six, roughly the third the industry figure describes. The three caught are all static, structural, single-element checks. The three missed all require either judging meaning (is this alt text good), simulating interaction over time (does Tab escape), or comparing two different representations of the page against each other (visual versus DOM order). None of those three is a smaller or rarer bug category than the first three — they're just invisible to a tool that only reads markup once and moves on.

contentSections.body: A green automated scan means the syntactic third of the work is done, not that the audit is done. Everything that requires judging meaning, simulating a real interaction sequence, or comparing what's rendered against what's in the DOM sits outside what any scanner can check by construction — and that two-thirds is exactly where a keyboard, a screen reader, and your own access needs, run by an actual person, earn their place in the workflow.
